extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Kant, philosophy of teleology, and philosophy of biology
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply Kant's criteria for teleological judgment and explanations of organised nature, including distinctions between mechanical and teleological causality, types of teleological theories, the notion of final purpose, and limits of physico-theology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of two kinds of causality
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between mechanical causality (nature's conformity to law) and teleological causality (an Idea which limits nature to a particular form), and this duality is not fully comprehended by Reason but must be acknowledged in discussing organised beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanical causality to account for phenomena according to laws of nature; acknowledge teleological causality when explaining internally purposive organised beings, while recognizing the supersensible substrate where Reason cannot determine positive grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of mechanical connection for phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: As regards phenomena, 'all that we assume as belonging to this nature (phenomenon) and as its product, must be thought as connected therewith according to mechanical laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when employing teleological explanations, do not abandon the mechanical principle for empirical investigation; mechanical causality retains force for explaining phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasionalism vs Pre-established Harmony as bases for purposive production
rubrics_metrics.description: If teleological production is assumed, its basis may be either Occasionalism (Supreme Cause directly furnishes organic formation on each occasion) or Pre-established Harmony (original products supplied capacities enabling reproduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Occasionalism as philosophically problematic because it 'loses' natural explanations and is unattractive to philosophers; prefer explanations that preserve nature's role where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of preformation theories: individual preformation (evolution/involution) vs epigenesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-established Harmony can be understood as individual preformation (theory of evolution/involution: generations as educts) or epigenesis (generations as products, generic preformation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise empirical difficulties of individual preformation (e.g., hybrids) and the relative empirical superiority of epigenesis prior to proof; prefer epigenesis as it treats nature as self-producing rather than purely preformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigenesis as preferable teleological interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Epigenesis regards nature as self-producing (not merely self-evolving) and, with minimal supernatural intervention after an original organisation, leaves subsequent development to natural processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor epigenesis for its economy of supernatural invention and its conformity with reflective Reason's inclination to explain propagation teleologically while minimizing appeals to direct divine intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blumenbach's formative impulse distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: In physical explanations of organised formations, there is an undeterminable yet unmistakable element (a 'formative impulse') distinct from the merely mechanical formative power universally resident in matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accounting for the origin of organised matter, allow for a conceptually distinct formative principle while still subjecting it to higher guidance and limiting presumptuous employment of teleological explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal purposiveness (organisms as ends in themselves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal purposiveness is that by which an object's possibility is bound up with being a purpose in itself (we can ask of an organised being 'What is it for?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal purposiveness to characterise organisms as natural purposes whose possibility invites teleological judgment about their form and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: External purposiveness (things as means)
rubrics_metrics.description: External purposiveness refers to how one thing of nature serves another as a means to a purpose; only organised beings can be ends toward which others are means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ascribe final-purpose status to non-organised things; evaluate external purposiveness only relative to organised beings for which they function as means (e.g., water as means for organisms, not for mountains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited applicability of purposiveness across nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every natural object can be regarded as final purpose of creation; examination of nature shows no being that has claim to being the final purpose, and what might be thought as ultimate purpose still cannot be a final purpose as a natural thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating apparent purposive arrangements with an ultimate natural purpose; recognize limits of attributing final-purpose status within nature itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective Judgement vs Determinant Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The teleological and mechanical principles used here are principles of the reflective Judgement about nature's production of forms (they do not determine the origin of beings in themselves but guide how we must represent them), i.e., teleological judgment is reflective, not determinant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying teleological judgment, treat it as a regulative mode for ordering phenomena and seeking unity of principles, not as a proof of ontological origins; remain open to mechanical explanations and invited to attempt them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man as natural purpose and candidate for ultimate purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: For reflective Judgement we may judge man to be not merely a natural purpose but the ultimate purpose of nature on earth, because he can form a concept of purposes and use Reason to create systems of purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceive man as potential final purpose only insofar as he possesses understanding and the moral will to be an end in himself; do not ground this claim purely in natural facts about man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between happiness and culture as candidate ultimate purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Two possible 'ultimate purposes' for man: (1) happiness (an empirical, variable Idea) and (2) culture (the aptitude and skill for setting and pursuing arbitrary purposes), with culture being the appropriate ultimate purpose Natura can be said to further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject happiness as a viable ultimate purpose because it is empirical, variable, and unattainable as a universal law; treat culture (development of capacity for purposiveness and freedom) as the legitimate teleological end nature may serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture comprises skill and discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture has two conditions: culture of skill (development of aptitudes to further purposes) and discipline (freeing of the will from the despotism of desires); both are necessary for the development of humanity toward final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cultural development by presence of both technical/artistic skills and moral discipline (ability to subordinate inclinations to reason); note that skill often depends on social inequality while discipline is fostered by hardships and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final purpose defined as unconditioned
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'final purpose' is one which needs no other as condition of its possibility; only a being with unconditioned legislation (noumenal man as moral agent) can be posited as a final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that any candidate final purpose be independent of further natural conditions; restrict claim of final-purpose status to noumenal moral agents rather than natural objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Physico-theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Physico-theology (inferring the Supreme Cause from purposes of nature) can justify the concept of an intelligent World Cause empirically but cannot disclose a final purpose of creation or determine properties of a Deity beyond empirical effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physico-theology narrowly: it explains teleological ordering as grounds for inferring a designer as a subjective concept of our cognitive faculty, but do not treat it as providing a full theology or as proving God's properties; supplementary moral-practical reasons (moral theology) are required for fuller theistic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Idealism of final causes (Pantheism/Spinozism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing purposiveness to mere ontological inherence in a single Substance (idealism of final causes leading to Pantheism/Spinozism) explains away rather than solves the question of the first ground of purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject accounts that eliminate purposive reality by transforming it into abstract ontological unity; maintain the distinction between teleological explanation and metaphysical idealism when seeking the ground of purposiveness.
